overview: The atlas’s “Hunters-gatherers” layer is not one civilization. Its 4000 and 3000 BCE files join Madagascar to Sardinia; the 2000 BCE file keeps only Sardinia. These low-precision island shapes do not identify a people, language, polity, or shared network. Sardinia is misnamed: ancient genomes, crops, livestock, pottery, villages, rock-cut collective tombs, copper working, and monuments document settled farming and herding communities. Madagascar poses a different problem. One rockshelter study proposed microlith-using foragers before 2000 BCE, while reanalysis argues that disturbed deposits, ambiguous bone damage, and the wider archaeological, ecological, genetic, and linguistic record support settlement much later. The disagreement must remain visible; a colored island cannot referee it. Even where foraging is securely attested, “hunter-gatherer” covers extraordinarily varied economies, mobility, families, politics, and technologies. This card therefore explains the atlas artifact, presents securely dated Sardinian evidence, labels contested Madagascan claims, and uses modern forager studies only to show possibilities and cautions. It does not manufacture a continent-spanning culture, prehistoric names, dialogue, school system, medicine cabinet, or municipal plumbing from a generic label.

periods.title: Two islands, no single people
periods.summary: The first available atlas snapshot joins all of Madagascar to Sardinia. Sardinian archaeology already documents agriculture, livestock, pottery, and stable settlement, while no securely contextualized Madagascan community can be described for these centuries. The combined label is an editorial category, not a discovered alliance.

periods.title: Sardinian communities build lasting places
periods.summary: Across Sardinia, Neolithic farming and herding communities lived in stable settlements using pottery and stone tools. By the 3200 BCE boundary, evidence enters the Ozieri phase, not throughout this entire period. Madagascar remains separate, so matching map color cannot make Mediterranean and Indian Ocean households contemporaries or cousins.

periods.title: Ozieri traditions and rock-cut tombs
periods.summary: Late Neolithic Sardinian communities carved collective tombs, produced elaborate pottery, and used caves and settlements in varied ways. The evidence supports named archaeological phases rather than generic foragers. Domus de janas imitate houses of the living, although they are mortuary architecture, not preserved bedrooms.

periods.title: A redraw is not a migration
periods.summary: The 3000 BCE file redraws coordinates slightly but retains Madagascar and Sardinia as two disconnected components. On Sardinia, Anghelu Ruju began long use across changing archaeological phases. Neither the map seam nor shared fill demonstrates travel between the islands or one uninterrupted social identity.

periods.title: Copper Age skills expand
periods.summary: Sardinian communities mined and worked copper, maintained farming and herding, and developed varied settlement and mortuary practices. Archaeologists see rising social and economic complexity, not a simple survival stage. The atlas label hides these local histories behind a broad subsistence word.

periods.title: Monte Claro marks regional change
periods.summary: Distinctive vessels and burial contexts define the Monte Claro archaeological phase around 2400 to 2100 BCE. Such phases organize material patterns; they are not automatic ethnic names. Madagascar remains on the atlas until 2000 BCE even though its proposed early human chronology is sharply disputed.

periods.title: Madagascar disappears from the layer
periods.summary: At 2000 BCE the atlas removes Madagascar and leaves Sardinia. A rockshelter study proposed earlier foragers, but reanalysis highlights disturbed sediments and dispersed dating. The cartographic change is therefore neither a documented migration nor an extinction; it is a silent editorial choice amid unresolved evidence.

periods.title: Early Bronze Age Sardinia outgrows the label
periods.summary: Bonnanaro sites document early Bronze Age communities and continued reuse of older tombs. At 1500 BCE the exact id vanishes during a broad atlas repaint. That endpoint does not end Sardinian life; it closes an inaccurate residual category as new archaeological traditions developed.

sections.title: Read the category and map critically

items.text: “Hunter-gatherer” names a subsistence emphasis, not a civilization, ethnicity, language, or rank on a ladder. Archaeologists debate the category because past foragers were more diverse than surviving comparisons suggest. Shared ways of obtaining food do not create a shared government, origin story, or border.

Madagascar’s settlement chronology is unusually unresolved. Reviews find early cutmarked bones and rockshelter dates difficult to interpret because context, stratigraphy, and dating disagree. A responsible card shows the disagreement; it does not let one polygon transform a contested visit, occupation, or natural mark into a civilization.

Faunal and environmental records describe an island rich in endemic animals long before securely dated settlements. Human hunting, climate variability, habitat change, and later introduced species require separate tests. “Animals existed here” cannot be shortened to “this mapped people hunted them,” however tempting the illustrated menu.

Madagascar contains highlands, rainforests, dry forests, wetlands, and coasts with different seasonal risks. Scholarly histories stress multiple arrivals and adaptations. Treating the entire island as one camp ignores landscape scale; treating it as the same society as Sardinia adds an ocean-sized second mistake.

The decoded 4000 and 3000 BCE features contain exactly two disconnected components: Madagascar and Sardinia. At 2000 BCE only Sardinia remains. No encoded arc touches another label, and all tested mainland cities fall outside. The visual category is literally two islands, not Africa and Europe filled edge to edge.

sections.title: Live in very different island environments

items.text: Pollen, sediment, and land-use models show that Sardinian vegetation changed with climate and human activity. These reconstructions are probabilistic and must be compared with excavated plants, animals, and settlements. A greener interval does not automatically reveal who cleared, grazed, gathered, or burned a particular hillside.

Madagascar’s wet east, dry southwest, central highlands, rivers, coasts, and seasonal rainfall produced sharply different habitats. Late-Holocene research separates regional hydroclimate from human pressure. One island outline therefore cannot supply a single food calendar, mobility pattern, or ecological impact for every location.

Sardinia’s tombs occur across coasts, mountains, plateaus, hills, and plains, often near settlements. Their wide distribution shows communities adapting a shared mortuary idea to local geology and livelihoods. It also warns that “Sardinian” is a geographic convenience, not proof that every village behaved identically.

Climate shapes opportunities without writing scripts for people. Madagascar’s faunal declines and Sardinia’s land use both require dated local evidence. Communities could respond by moving, storing, exchanging, changing crops, managing herds, or revising rituals. Environmental stress is a question to investigate, not an all-purpose historical puppet master.

Island living never meant isolation. Seas could obstruct travel, but boats also connected coasts, materials, people, and ideas. The evidence for each voyage must be dated and sourced. The atlas supplies no route between Madagascar and Sardinia; drawing the same color is not ancient ferry service.

sections.title: Grow, gather, herd, fish, and cook

items.text: Charred plant remains from Sardinia identify domesticated cereals and legumes and reveal crop processing. This is direct evidence for farming work, storage decisions, and food preparation, although preservation is uneven. The island’s atlas label misses the hoes-and-harvest side of life before anyone reaches the hunting scene.

Su Mulinu Mannu’s Middle Neolithic context dates about 4500 to 4100 BCE, before this atlas interval. It preserves free-threshing wheat, naked and hulled barley, and wild plants. The site cannot describe a 3800 BCE meal; it establishes that diversified cultivation already preceded the layer’s opening.

The pottery study concerns contexts dated 4500 to 4000 BCE, ending at this layer’s boundary. Vessel form, wear, residues, and isotopes document ruminant fats, plant foods, non-ruminant products, and aquatic resources in Sardinian kitchens. It supplies background at 4000 BCE, not a direct menu for later centuries.

A large stable-isotope synthesis finds prehistoric Italian diets generally combined terrestrial protein and C3 plants, with greater Copper Age variation. Isotopes measure patterned consumption in sampled bodies, not named recipes. They cannot tell whether someone preferred stew, flatbread, or the prehistoric equivalent of picking around dinner.

At Scaba e Arriu, burial phases dated about 3400 to 2600 and 2700 to 2350 BCE provide isotope evidence about cattle, sheep, goats, pigs, and animal products. They support settled agropastoral lives during those phases; they cannot describe every Sardinian community or extend unchanged beyond 2350 BCE.

sections.title: Build homes and move for reasons

items.text: Sardinian Neolithic evidence includes stable settlements built around agriculture, livestock, pottery, and stone tools. People still moved between fields, pastures, quarries, coasts, kin, and ceremonies. “Settled” never means motionless, just as “mobile” never means wandering without plans, landmarks, or a place to return.

Monte d’Accoddi developed through a sequence from roughly 3200 to 2600 BCE: an earlier altar about 3200 to 2800, rebuilding near 2800, and village huts around 2600. Its ramped monuments and repeated construction show coordinated labor over centuries, rather than one completed complex standing simultaneously in 3000 BCE.

Madagascar’s early rockshelter chronology is contested partly because objects and dated sediments may have moved through bioturbation. A stone tool can establish human action; its position must establish when. Archaeology is careful about this because a burrowing animal can be an extremely energetic, if unhelpful, assistant excavator.

Modern Mikea communities combine foraging with cultivation and carry mixed African and Austronesian ancestry. Research describes recent cultural change, not a fossil survival from 2000 BCE. Their lives can challenge stereotypes about fixed subsistence identities, but cannot fill the atlas interval by ethnographic time travel.

Transitions from foraging toward village farming were often gradual and reversible, with mobility, hunting, managed plants, architecture, and ritual changing at different speeds. This wider pattern helps ask questions. Sardinia’s own settlements and burials must answer them; a universal evolutionary staircase cannot.

sections.title: Make tools, exchange materials, and innovate

items.text: Monte Arci obsidian was quarried, selected, worked, and shaped into blades, scrapers, points, and other tools. Finds across Sardinia and beyond support distribution, while scholars debate how organized exchange was. The production chain demonstrates geological knowledge and skilled hands, not a generic “Stone Age” pause button.

Copper Age Sardinians located ores and learned to extract and work metal, while stone, bone, wood, clay, and fibers remained useful. Metallurgy added choices rather than instantly replacing older technologies. Later bronze mastery should not be projected backward, but its Copper Age foundations deserve recognition.

Menhirs, dolmens, rock-cut tombs, sanctuaries, caves, and settlements show several architectural traditions coexisting in Sardinia. Quarrying, cutting, hauling, decorating, and maintaining these places required accumulated expertise. The achievement belongs to many communities; the atlas’s single label makes that teamwork look unnecessarily anonymous.

The pottery study’s vessels come from contexts dated 4500 to 4000 BCE, at or before this layer’s opening. Analysis examines form, wear, residues, and isotopes rather than guessing from decoration alone. Beautiful pots also did unglamorous kitchen duty, but they cannot document ceramic change through later centuries.

The proposed Lakaton’i Anja microliths would indicate skilled stone reduction and coastal foraging if their early association holds. Later critiques dispute the deposit dates, not the fact that the objects were made. The correct discovery story includes both technological observation and the unresolved clock.

Collective Sardinian tombs held multiple people and were reopened across generations. That practice suggests durable communities of remembrance, but a chamber is not a complete household census. Biological relatives, spouses, neighbors, ritual affiliates, and selected dead may overlap without producing one tidy modern family diagram.

Ancient mitochondrial genomes sample maternal lineages, not whole societies. Sardinian data show diversity and broad continuity across some phases, yet burial selection and small samples matter. Genes can reveal biological relationships and population history; they cannot identify a person’s job, jokes, political loyalties, or preferred pottery.

Modern genomic structure on Sardinia reflects ancient and recent processes, including early farmer ancestry and regional isolation. Present people are not unchanged Neolithic communities. Converting ancestry components into named prehistoric tribes would confuse statistical models with lived identities, marriage networks, languages, and historical change.

Cooperative childcare is widespread but varies with ecology, demography, kinship, and reciprocity. Comparative research supplies possibilities, not Sardinian nursery rules. Archaeology can identify children and shared places; it rarely records who soothed a baby at midnight or negotiated the Bronze Age version of bedtime.

Mikea research shows that subsistence identity can shift within recent history and that foragers remain connected to farmers, markets, and wider Malagasy society. This undercuts the myth of sealed-off hunter-gatherer bands. It also prevents using living Mikea social organization as a template for undated prehistoric islanders.

sections.title: Raise children and pass on knowledge

items.text: Comparative studies find children learning by observation, participation, play, practice, and direct teaching, with peers and older children often important. These patterns show what human learning can look like. They do not recover a Sardinian timetable, and “no school building” never means “no education.”

By early childhood, many forager children in comparative studies learn everyday skills such as tool handling, food preparation, infant care, cooking, sharing, and plant knowledge. The exact age and teacher vary. This evidence argues against imagining passive childhood, while remaining an analogy rather than a Sardinian diary.

Research across twelve forager and mixed-subsistence societies finds large differences in children’s time spent playing, caring, producing food, and doing domestic work. Safe, abundant resources can support child contribution. Diversity is the useful lesson; one global childhood model would repeat the atlas’s flattening mistake.

Alloparents can include siblings, grandparents, other kin, and non-kin, but who helps depends on social and ecological circumstances. Cooperative care may buffer risk. Without direct Sardinian evidence, the careful conclusion is that caregiving involved relationships, not that every tomb group followed one universal family recipe.

Collective tomb and ancient-DNA records preserve selected people and practices rather than a child’s daily routine. Archaeologists can compare body treatment, objects, tomb reuse, ancestry, and biological relationships where sampled. These sources identify no formal schools, textbooks, or interval literacy; precise learning arrangements remain undocumented.

sections.title: Treat illness, injury, and care cautiously

items.text: Scaba e Arriu’s isotope study concerns burial phases dated about 3400 to 2600 and 2700 to 2350 BCE. It reconstructs aspects of food and mobility more securely than medical treatment. Isotopes are valuable witnesses, but they do not turn a person’s remains into a full medical chart.

Two Mesolithic Sardinian genomes come from people thousands of years before this card, and later samples remain limited. They show why biological evidence needs dates and context. Ancient DNA can identify ancestry and kinship patterns; it does not diagnose every illness or transmit a community’s healing knowledge.

Genomic continuity does not mean bodies escaped disease, hunger, injury, or unequal care. Population-level models average individuals and cannot substitute for skeleton-by-skeleton study. Likewise, genetic similarity never proves a shared healer, remedy, or belief across villages, centuries, and different archaeological phases.

No securely identified Sardinian medical text survives from 4000 to 1500 BCE. Plants, splints, massage, heat, food, rest, skilled birth assistance, and ritual care are possible, but specific prescriptions would be invented. Evidence of survival after injury can suggest support without naming the treatment.

Madagascar’s disputed early chronology means we cannot responsibly reconstruct interval medicine, childbirth, disability care, or healers there. Much later Malagasy practices belong to later communities. The humane choice is precision: acknowledging missing evidence respects real people better than furnishing them with a fictional medicine basket.

sections.title: Find water, manage waste, and face the toilet question

items.text: The cited South Korean review reports no identified Neolithic toilet structures there; researchers instead use coprolites and middens. That comparison cannot prove Sardinian or Madagascan sanitation. No dedicated interval facility is documented in this packet’s island sources, so exact bathroom rules remain unknown, and archaeology has not recovered the policy manual.

Su Mulinu Mannu’s plant remains and the pottery study’s residues come from contexts dated 4500 to 4000 BCE, before or at this layer’s boundary. Such deposits teach how archaeologists distinguish food preparation, discard, fill, and unusual deposition. Archaeological “trash” is evidence, but a broken pot carries no rubbish label.

Monte d’Accoddi’s 3200 to 2600 BCE sequence included monuments, rebuilding, and village huts, creating changing needs for water, clay, plaster, food, people, and animals. The site account documents no municipal sewer. Daily water carrying was infrastructure, although its people, containers, routes, and schedules remain archaeologically indistinct.

Tombs occur near settlements across varied Sardinian terrain, so communities had to manage living areas, animals, food waste, and the dead in spatially meaningful ways. Exact disposal customs are not uniform or fully known. Mapping tombs cannot locate the nearest drinking spring or discreet bathroom spot.

For Madagascar, unsettled occupation dates make interval sanitation claims especially unsafe. A possible short visit, seasonal camp, and permanent village would leave different waste patterns. Before asking where people put refuse or excrement, archaeology must establish that people were present, when, and for how long.

sections.title: Create art, remember the dead, and avoid fake writing

items.text: Sardinian communities carved, painted, and engraved tombs, raised stones, built dolmens, and organized sanctuaries. Motifs and architecture express relationships with bodies, places, animals, and ancestors without providing a written transcript. Similar forms around the Mediterranean suggest interaction, while local combinations remained distinctive.

Domus de janas imitate beams, roofs, doors, and other features of houses, sometimes with red ochre and horn motifs. Their later nickname means “fairy houses,” not the builders’ recorded term. The tombs illuminate memory and domestic imagery; they do not preserve a prehistoric caption explaining every symbol.

Written sample: none can be securely supplied for this interval. Sardinia’s earliest known written document is the Phoenician Nora stele, dated roughly 850 to 725 BCE, centuries later. Earlier motifs are meaningful images, not a deciphered script, and Madagascar has no securely associated interval text.

Modern Malagasy populations carry heterogeneous African and Asian ancestry shaped by much later movements. Malagasy languages and identities cannot be projected back onto an uncertain 4000 to 2000 BCE presence. Later evidence explains living diversity; it does not reveal the speech of hypothetical early visitors.

Mikea are contemporary Malagasy people with mixed ancestry and flexible histories of farming and foraging. Calling them surviving members of the atlas layer would deny both evidence and modern identity. Continuity can involve landscapes and practices without turning living communities into museum exhibits from an invented prehistoric civilization.

ending.text: At approximately 1500 BCE the atlas deletes `hunters-gatherers` during a broad repaint of Africa and Europe. Nothing in the source files documents a conquest, migration, demographic collapse, or collective decision to change livelihoods. Sardinia had already supported farming and herding communities, monuments, collective tombs, pottery, obsidian networks, and copper work; its early Bronze Age Bonnanaro phases continued into the atlas endpoint and helped precede Nuragic developments. Madagascar had disappeared from this label five centuries earlier, but that seam cannot resolve the island’s fiercely debated settlement chronology. Securely documented Malagasy population history belongs much later and joins African and Austronesian ancestries through complex movements. For both islands, an editorial label ends while human and environmental histories continue. No successor is assigned because one invented cross-oceanic population cannot sensibly transform into another. The safest conclusion is also the most interesting: the map’s empty category dissolves, Sardinian communities keep changing, Madagascar’s archaeological question remains open to better dates and contexts, and living island peoples are not leftovers from a colored polygon. Someone misplaced the label; nobody misplaced two islands.
